title: Chunk Atlas — Real-Time Fluency: Under Fire

questions.question: You've just been asked a direct question you genuinely don't know the answer to, in front of others. Which chunk fits best?

options.A: Can I come back to you?
options.B: Can I have thirty seconds on that?
options.C: One second, let me land this.
options.D: Can I park the second question and come back to it?

questions.explanation:
✓ Correct — "Can I come back to you?" is an Admitting you don't know, with a next step chunk: used to admit you don't know something confidently, while committing to a next step.
Example: "Can I come back to you on the exact figure? I don't want to misquote it."
Similar chunks:
- I don't want to guess and give you the wrong answer.
- I don't know — but I'll find out and come back to you by [time].
- I don't have that off the top of my head. Can I follow up this afternoon?

✗ "Can I have thirty seconds on that?" belongs to Buying structured thinking time when put on the spot — used to buy structured thinking time out loud, right after being put on the spot, not this context.
Similar chunks:
- Can you come back to me at the end?
- I'd have to look.
- I'd rather give you a considered answer than a fast one.

✗ "One second, let me land this." belongs to Holding the floor when talked over — used to hold onto your turn when someone talks over you, not this context.
Similar chunks:
- Hang on — I'm almost there.
- I'd like to finish.
- Let me finish this point.

✗ "Can I park the second question and come back to it?" belongs to Handling multiple questions at once — used to organize your response when someone asks several questions at once, not this context.
Similar chunks:
- There are three questions there. Let me take them one at a time.
- Let me start with the last one, because it's the most important.
- Which of those matters most to you? I'll start there.
